title: Elephants, storks and the phoenix
source_text: Οὐκ οἶδα δ᾿ ὅπως ὁ Κέλσος καὶ ὅρκου ἐλεφάντων ἤκουσε, καὶ ὅτι εἰσὶν οὗτοι πιστότεροι πρὸς τὸ θεῖον ἡμῶν καὶ γνῶσιν ἔχουσι τοῦ θεοῦ. ἐγὼ γὰρ πολλὰ μὲν καὶ θαυμαστὰ οἶδα περὶ τῆς φύσεως τοῦ ζῴου καὶ τῆς ἡμερότητος ἱστορούμενα. οὐ μὴν καὶ περὶ ὅρκων ἐλέφαντος σύνοιδα εἰρῆσθαι παρά τινι· εἰ μὴ ἄρα τὸ ἥμερον καὶ τὴν ὡσπερεὶ πρὸς ἀνθρώπους αὐτῶν συνθήκην ἅπαξ γενομένων ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῖς εὐορκίαν τηρουμένην ὠνόμασεν, ὅπερ καὶ αὐτὸ ψεῦδός ἐστιν. εἰ γὰρ καὶ σπανίως, ἀλλ᾿ οὖν γε ἱστόρηται ὅτι μετὰ τὴν δοκοῦσαν ἡμερότητα ἐξηγριώθησαν ἐλέφαντες κατὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων (καὶ φόνους ἐποίησαν) καὶ διὰ τοῦτο κατεδικάσθησαν ἀναιρεθῆναι ὡς οὐκέτι χρήσιμοι. ἐπεὶ δὲ παραλαμβάνει μετὰ ταῦτα εἰς τὸ κατασκευάσαι, ὡς οἴεται, εὐσεβεστέρους εἶναι τοὺς πελαργοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὰ περὶ τοῦ ζῴου ἱστορούμενα, ἀντιπελαργοῦντος καὶ τροφὰς φέροντος τοῖς γεγεννηκόσι· λεκτέον ὅτι καὶ τοῦτ᾿ οὐκ ἀπὸ θεωρήματος τοῦ περὶ τοῦ καθήκοντος ποιοῦσιν οἱ πελαργοὶ οὐδ᾿ ἀπὸ λογισμοῦ ἀλλ᾿ ἀπὸ φύσεως. βουληθείσης τῆς κατασκευαζούσης αὐτοὺς φύσεως παράδειγμα ἐν ἀλόγοις ζῴοις δυσωπῆσαι δυνάμενον ἀνθρώπους ἐκθέσθαι περὶ τοῦ χάριτας ἀποτιννύειν τοῖς γεγεννηκόσιν. εἰ δὲ ᾔδει Κέλσος, ὅσῳ διαφέρει λόγῳ ταῦτα ποιεῖν τοῦ ἀλόγως καὶ φυσικῶς αὐτὰ ἐνεργεῖν, οὐκ ἂν εὐσεβεστέρους εἶπε τοὺς πελαργοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἔτι δὲ ὡς ὑπὲρ εὐσεβείας τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων ἱστάμενος ὁ Κέλσος παραλαμβάνει τὸ Ἀράβιον ζῷον, τὸν φοίνικα. διὰ πολλῶν ἐτῶν ἐπιδημοῦν Αἰγύπτῳ καὶ φέρον ἀποθανόντα τὸν πατέρα καὶ ταφέντα ἐν σφαίρᾳ σμύρνης καὶ ἐπιτιθὲν ὅπου τὸ τοῦ ἡλίου τέμενος, καὶ τοῦτο δὲ ἱστόρηται μὲν δύναται δὲ, ἐάνπερ ᾖ ἀληθὲς, καὶ αὐτὸ φυσικὸν τυγχάνειν, ἐπιδαψιλευσαμένης τῆς θείας προνοίας καὶ ἐν ταῖς διαφοραῖς τῶν ζῴων παραστῆσαι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τὸ ποικίλον τῆς τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ κατασκευῆς φθάνον καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρνεα· καὶ ζῷόν τι „μονογενὲς“ ὑπέστησεν. ἵνα καὶ τοῦτο ποιήσῃ θαυμασθῆναι οὐ τὸ ζῷον ἀλλὰ τὸν πεποιηκότα αὐτό.
pass_a_gloss: I do not know (οὐκ οἶδα) how Celsus heard (ἤκουσε) even of an oath (ὅρκος) of elephants (ἐλέφας), and that these are more faithful (πιστότεροι) toward the divine (τὸ θεῖον) than we and have knowledge (γνῶσις) of God. For I know many and wonderful (θαυμαστά) things recorded (ἱστορούμενα) about the nature (φύσις) of the animal and its tameness (ἡμερότης); yet I am not aware (σύνοιδα) that anything about oaths of an elephant has been said by anyone; unless perhaps he named (ὠνόμασεν) the tame [quality] (τὸ ἥμερον) and their compact (συνθήκη), as it were (ὡσπερεί), toward men, kept once they have come under them, 'oath-keeping' (εὐορκία); which itself is a falsehood (ψεῦδος). For even if rarely, yet it is recorded that after their seeming (δοκοῦσα) tameness elephants turned savage (ἐξηγριώθησαν) against men (and made murders, φόνους) and for this were condemned (κατεδικάσθησαν) to be destroyed (ἀναιρεθῆναι) as no longer useful (χρήσιμοι). Since after these things he adduces (παραλαμβάνει), to establish (κατασκευάσαι), as he thinks, that storks (πελαργοί) are more pious (εὐσεβέστεροι) than men, the things recorded about the animal, [namely] its returning care (ἀντιπελαργέω) and bringing food (τροφαί) to those who begot it (οἱ γεγεννηκότες): it must be said (λεκτέον) that this too storks do not from a theorem/considered principle (θεώρημα) about duty (τὸ καθῆκον) nor from reasoning (λογισμός) but from nature, the nature constructing them (ἡ κατασκευάζουσα φύσις) having wished (βουληθείσης) to set forth (ἐκθέσθαι) in irrational animals (ἄλογα ζῷα) an example (παράδειγμα) able to shame (δυσωπῆσαι) men about repaying thanks (χάριτας ἀποτιννύειν) to those who begot them. If Celsus had known (ᾔδει) how much doing these things by reason (λόγῳ) differs (διαφέρει) from performing (ἐνεργεῖν) them irrationally (ἀλόγως) and naturally (φυσικῶς), he would not have called storks more pious than men. Further, as standing up for (ἱστάμενος ὑπέρ) the piety of irrational animals, Celsus adduces the Arabian animal, the phoenix (φοῖνιξ), visiting (ἐπιδημοῦν) Egypt through many years and carrying its father dead and buried in a ball (σφαῖρα) of myrrh (σμύρνα) and placing [him] where the precinct (τέμενος) of the sun is; and this too is recorded, but it can, if indeed it is true, itself also be natural (φυσικόν), divine providence (ἡ θεία πρόνοια) having been lavish (ἐπιδαψιλευσαμένης) also in the differences of animals to present to men the variety of the construction of things in the world, reaching even to birds; and it established a certain 'only-begotten' animal, so that by this too it might cause to be wondered at not the animal but the one who made it.
pass_b_english: I do not know how Celsus came to hear even of an oath sworn by elephants, and that they are more faithful toward the divine than we are, and have knowledge of God. For I know many wonderful things that are recorded about the nature of this animal and its tameness, but I am not aware that anyone has spoken of an elephant’s oaths. Unless, perhaps, he has given the name of oath-keeping to their tameness, and to the compact, as it were, which they keep with men once they have come under men’s control; and even that is false. For it is recorded, if only rarely, that elephants which seemed tame have turned savage against men and killed people, and for this were condemned to be put to death as no longer of use.

After this he brings in what is recorded about the stork, that it repays its parents’ care and carries food to those who begot it, in order to prove, as he supposes, that storks are more pious than men. To this we must say that storks do this too not from a considered grasp of duty, nor from reasoning, but from nature. The nature that formed them wished to set forth, in animals without reason, an example that could shame men into repaying the kindness of those who begot them. If Celsus had known how great the difference is between doing these things by reason and performing them without reason, by nature, he would not have said that storks are more pious than men.

Further, as though he were standing up for the piety of animals without reason, Celsus brings in the Arabian creature, the phoenix: at intervals of many years it visits Egypt, bringing its father, who has died and been buried in a ball of myrrh, and lays him down where the precinct of the sun is. This too is recorded. But if it is true, it may also be a work of nature. For divine providence has been lavish in setting before men, in the differences among living things as well, the variety in the ordering of what is in the world, a variety that reaches even to the birds; and it has brought into being a certain “only-begotten” creature, so that by this too it might cause men to wonder not at the creature but at the One who made it.

choices.choice: Removed quotation marks from the elephant claim: Greek gives it as Origen's indirect report (ὅτι + οὗτοι), not Celsus's quoted words
'that anyone has said anything about the oaths of an elephant' -> 'that anyone has spoken of an elephant's oaths' (dropped added 'anything')
'once they have come under their control' -> 'under men's control' (ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῖς = under men; removed ambiguity)
'committed murders' -> 'killed people' (φόνους ἐποίησαν, natural English for animals)
'set before us' -> 'set forth' (ἐκθέσθαι; Greek has no 'us')
'repaying gratitude to those who begot them' -> 'repaying the kindness of those who begot them' (χάριτας ἀποτιννύειν; removed calque)
'after many years it comes to Egypt' -> 'at intervals of many years it visits Egypt' (διὰ πολλῶν ἐτῶν ἐπιδημοῦν = periodic visit)

Celsus's words: the claim about elephants (πιστότεροι πρὸς τὸ θεῖον ἡμῶν καὶ γνῶσιν ἔχουσι τοῦ θεοῦ) is given by Origen as reported speech after ὅτι, with his own pointer οὗτοι, and Celsus's original wording does not survive in the staged Book 4 rows; reviewer removed the quotation marks so the English follows the Greek frame (indirect report). The stork and phoenix descriptions are woven into Origen's own sentences (participles agreeing with his nouns), so they are kept as indirect report without quotation marks. 'And killed people' (καὶ φόνους ἐποίησαν) is an editorial supplement in brackets in the staged Koetschau text; translated without marking. ἀντιπελαργέω (literally 'to stork in return') = to care for one's parents in turn; rendered 'repays its parents' care'. θεώρημα περὶ τοῦ καθήκοντος: Stoic language for a reasoned grasp of what is fitting/duty; rendered 'a considered grasp of duty'. διὰ πολλῶν ἐτῶν: at intervals of many years (the periodic visit of the phoenix). τέμενος τοῦ ἡλίου: the Sun's sacred precinct (Heliopolis in the familiar phoenix story, cf. Herodotus 2.73, which tells the myrrh-egg story; Origen does not quote Herodotus, so no inline citation). μονογενές stands in quotation marks in Koetschau: 'only-begotten', i.e. the single bird of its kind; the same word is applied to the phoenix in 1 Clement 25.2, which may be the source of the quotation marks. It is the Johannine title of the Son (John 1:14, 18; 3:16), but here it describes the bird and is not a Scripture allusion, so it carries no citation. 'The One who made it' is capitalised because ὁ πεποιηκώς refers to God the Creator (the subject is divine providence). No Scripture quotations or clear allusions in this chapter.
